newsitem.title: UK: UK consumer group attacks BA, American deal.
newsitem.headline: UK consumer group attacks BA, American deal.

text.p: British proposals for approving British Airways' planned alliance with American Airlines came under attack from an influential consumer group on Friday, adding to a growing chorus of opposition from other airlines.

Britain's Air Transport Users Council (ATUC) said it had told the Office of Fair Trading (OFT) that the proposals did not go far enough to allow other airlines to mount effective competition at London Heathrow, where BA and American currently operate over 70 percent of all transatlantic traffic.

The OFT has invited comments by 1700 GMT today on its proposals to allow the the deal to go ahead if BA and American make certain concessions, including releasing 168 of their weekly takeoff and landing slots at Heathrow -- enough to operate 12 daily return flights.
But the ATUC and rival airlines have all said more slots must be given up, and that BA should be forced to hand over the slots rather than sell them.

"The OFT proposals are inadequate to maintain competition on transatlantic routes out of London," ATUC chairman Ian Hamer said in a statement. "It is not enough to make the alliance give up slots -- their services need to be cut back to make room for new competitors."

The ATUC said it had suggested to the OFT that instead a three-year cap should be placed on the proportion of services that the alliance might operate on six transatlantic routes where the alliance would otherwise be dominant, and slots should be transferred for free, "or made available on a long period loan."

Meanwhile U.S. airline Delta Air Lines said it had told the OFT that the British conditions for approval were "completely inadequate" and that the alliance should be referred to the UK Monopolies and Mergers Commission for fuller investigation.
"In order to ensure effective competition to Heathrow, UK and U.S. carriers would require hundreds of additional slots," said Delta's European vice president Michael Medlicott.
Delta said that American Airlines and British Airways together currently had a total of 3,353 slots at Heathrow and U.S. carriers would need "at least 550 additional weekly slots."

The OFT said in its review of the alliance last month that together BA and American operated 490 weekly slots for transatlantic flights at Heathrow, 65 percent of all slots currently used for transatlantic services at the airport.
On Thursday Continental Airlines and United Airlines also called on the OFT to toughen up conditions for approving the deal.

Continental said it would require 140 weekly takeoff and landing slots at Heathrow along with adequate ground handling facilities to be able to mount effective competition on routes to New York and to Houston.
United, which unlike Continental already has an operation at Heathrow, said it was telling the OFT that BA and American should give up more slots and that it should give them for free.
"BA and American rather than the competing airlines, must pay the economic price for reducing competition in key markets," United said in a statement.

United said it was proposing to the OFT that BA and American should hand over sufficient slots to allow the introduction of 15 new daily transatlantic flights by other airlines -- equivalent to 210 weekly takeoff and landing slots.
The ATUC is an independent body funded by Britain's Civil Aviation Authority (CAA).
BA which is due to make its own submission to the OFT today says it should not be forced to give up slots, and any that are given up should be acquired by rivals "for a fair value."
